clue.text: It's difficult on board with smashed crockery

indicators.note: on board a ship means sitting inside the ship's letters, so this word puts one piece within the other

parts.note: being on board means being on a ship, and SS (steamship) is the crossword's usual ship
difficult means hard

explanation.surface: A clumsy passenger finds it hard going on a ship where the crockery keeps getting smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' and 'with' are link words; HARD goes aboard SS, the steamship abbreviation, giving S-HARD-S.
explanation.definitionFit: Shards are the sharp broken fragments left when pottery or glass is smashed.

clue.text: Flog in place of punishment, they say

indicators.note: they say signals that the word for the place of punishment is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a prison cell is a place of punishment

explanation.surface: Someone suggests that a flogging should replace imprisonment as the penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Flog is informal British slang for selling something, often quickly or cheaply.

clue.text: Goddess declares, a beginning and end of love

parts.note: a beginning is a start

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of the word love

explanation.surface: A goddess announces that love has both a start and a finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'declares' is a link word, standing for 'is' between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Astarte is the Phoenician goddess of fertility and love, the counterpart of Ishtar.

clue.text: Infected and died abroad

annotationWithheld.why: Infected and died abroad (8): DISEASED is DIED around SEAS, but 'abroad' must give both SEAS (overseas) and the containment, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: The complaint of King George lacking one laver

indicators.note: lacking tells us something is taken away from the illness's name

parts.note: King George III is thought to have suffered from porphyria, a blood disorder causing his madness
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: The illness of a mad monarch is said to have spared him one seaweed dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Laver is an edible red seaweed (eaten as laverbread in Wales), and Porphyra is its genus name.
explanation.definitionFit: Porphyra is the scientific genus of the red seaweeds sold as laver or nori.

clue.text: Dickensian served vitriol stew

indicators.note: served up, the letters are dished out in a new order like a meal

explanation.surface: A Victorian workhouse serves its inmates a stew so foul it tastes of acid.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting surface: the workhouse boy famously asked for more gruel.
explanation.definitionFit: The orphan hero of the novel Oliver Twist is a Dickensian character, one created by Charles Dickens.

clue.text: Glorification is seen in the rising of Wyatt

indicators.note: seen in places the little word is inside the other piece
in a down clue, rising means the name is read from the bottom upwards, backwards

parts.note: Wyatt Earp was the Wild West marshal of the OK Corral gunfight

explanation.surface: History praises the Tudor rebel Thomas Wyatt's uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wyatt' and 'rising' suggest the Tudor rebel Thomas Wyatt's revolt of 1554, but the Wyatt needed is the Wild West lawman; in a down clue 'the rising of' turns his surname upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Praise is the act of glorifying or extolling someone, so it is a synonym for glorification.

clue.text: Met weapon used on board?

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police, based at Scotland Yard
an arm is a weapon

explanation.surface: Asks whether a police weapon might be brought aboard ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardarm is the end of a spar on a sailing ship's mast, equipment found on board.

clue.text: Nutty type could be a mug, sadly

indicators.note: could be says the letters may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Someone who is a bit nuts might, sadly, turn out to be a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder; the signal is 'could be'.
explanation.definitionFit: Amygdalus is the botanical genus of the almond, so it is a nut-bearing type of tree.

clue.text: Hot news of state trial

parts.note: LA is the abbreviation for Louisiana, a US state
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: A breaking report about a state court case.
explanation.definitionFit: The latest is the most recent news, the freshest item just in.

clue.text: Chaos is to come shortly — in 24 hours

indicators.note: in places the other pieces inside the period of a day

parts.note: 24 hours make a day
to come is to arrive, abbreviated in timetables as arr.

explanation.surface: A warning that pandemonium will arrive within a day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' signals the abbreviation ARR (arrive, as on a timetable); IS and ARR sit inside DAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Disarray means a state of confusion and disorder, so it is a synonym for chaos.

clue.text: Wealth is real estate, which is novel

parts.note: treasure is accumulated wealth
real estate is land and the property on it

explanation.surface: A homily that property is true riches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which is' is a link joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Treasure Island is Robert Louis Stevenson's pirate adventure novel.

clue.text: It's rare to see Roger nude!

definitions.text: It's rare to see Roger nude!

parts.words: It's rare to see Roger nude!
parts.note: rare as in lightly cooked meat; a naked man named Roger Cook would be a Cook who is not dressed

explanation.surface: A remark that a man called Roger is seldom seen naked.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Cook was a well-known British TV investigative reporter; a nude Cook is an undressed one, and rare steak is not cooked through.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare meat is cooked only briefly, so it is food that has not been fully done.

clue.text: At the same time it's archaic

definitions.text: At the same time it's archaic

parts.words: At the same time it's archaic
parts.note: an old legal and commercial phrase meaning bearing the same date, now no longer in everyday use

explanation.surface: Something old-fashioned happening simultaneously.
explanation.definitionFit: The dated legal phrase describes documents bearing the same date, so they are at the same time.

clue.text: Frank could be anything in Yorkshire

parts.note: in Yorkshire dialect owt means anything, so an owt said aloud sounds like the first part of the word

explanation.surface: A blunt man could come from anywhere in Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire folk are famously blunt; 'owt' (anything) spoken gives OUT SPOKEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Outspoken means candid and blunt in speech, the same as frank.

clue.text: Erich Kästner's boy rejected fruit

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the fruit's name is read backwards

parts.note: a lime is a citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A German author's young son turns down a piece of fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Emil is the boy hero of Kästner's children's novel Emil and the Detectives.

clue.text: 7 thrashes — they were tough

parts.note: 7-down is a yardarm, which is a spar on a ship's mast
to tan someone's hide is to thrash them

explanation.surface: A ship's crew beats people with a yardarm, so they were hardy folk.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spartans of ancient Greece were famed for their austere and hardy military discipline.

clue.text: Conservative backing the centre was sacked

indicators.note: backing the centre means only the middle letters of the word are turned around

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A Tory who supported centrist politics lost his job.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle pair OR in TORY becomes RO. Troy, the Homeric city, was sacked by the Greeks.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient city in Homer was captured and plundered by the Greeks, a sacking.

clue.text: 14 misses turn perhaps more frequently

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the remaining letters might be arranged differently
misses means leaves out a letter

parts.note: the number itself spelt out in words
a turn could be a U-turn, giving the letter U

explanation.surface: Someone misses the turn on the fourteenth more often than not.
explanation.walkthrough: Here '14' is the number, not the cross-reference to EMIL; FOURTEEN without U leaves FORTEEN, which 'perhaps' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Oftener is the comparative of often, meaning on more occasions.

clue.text: Trousers designed for passing water

definitions.meaning: very narrow tight-legged trousers popular with 1950s Teddy boys
pipes carrying waste water away from a building

explanation.definitionFit: Narrow 1950s trousers took the name of the slim pipes that carry away rainwater.

clue.text: Reformed worker dropped complaint

indicators.note: dropped means the worker is left out of the word

parts.note: a Protestant belongs to a church of the Reformation
the ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: A rehabilitated employee was let go and grumbled about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed' looks like an anagram signal, but it stands for PROTESTANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A protest is an objection or complaint voiced against something.

clue.text: Amateur wrestling without point for injury

indicators.note: wrestling suggests the letters grappling into a new shape
without means the compass point is removed

parts.note: E for east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: An amateur wrestler without a single point gets hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A trauma is a physical wound or injury, as in medical usage.

clue.text: Classic prayer leading to contention in the City

indicators.note: leading to puts the prayer in front of the dispute

parts.note: the Paternoster is the Lord's Prayer in Latin, classic as in classical language
a row is a quarrel, a contention

explanation.surface: Saying a traditional prayer led to a dispute in the financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is the City of London; Paternoster Row, beside St Paul's Cathedral, was the old heart of London publishing.
explanation.definitionFit: Paternoster Row is a street in the City of London, near St Paul's.

clue.text: Eastern study of a politician

parts.note: a den is a private study or retreat

explanation.surface: An Oriental analysis of a statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was British Prime Minister 1955-57; 'of' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Eden was a Conservative statesman and British Prime Minister.

clue.text: County fortunate not to have started in America

parts.note: Kent is a county in south-east England

indicators.note: not to have started means the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: fortunate means lucky

explanation.surface: An English county lucky not to have begun in America.
explanation.definitionFit: Kentucky is a US state, so it is found in America.

clue.text: No more smoke?

parts.note: a cigarette stub, the bit left when there is nothing more to smoke; fag is British slang for cigarette

explanation.surface: A question about whether the cigarettes have run out.
explanation.definitionFit: The butt of a cigarette is the last remnant, with nothing more left to smoke.

clue.text: Boy turns on girl in France

indicators.note: turns means the boy's name is read backwards

parts.note: Ron is a boy's name
Mandy is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A lad rounds on his girlfriend while holidaying in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link word, placing one piece beside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Normandy is a region of northern France.

clue.text: Well known at Sadler's Wells, Mancunians speak of him with stress

definitions.text: Well known at Sadler's Wells, Mancunians speak of him with stress

parts.words: Well known at Sadler's Wells, Mancunians speak of him with stress
parts.note: a famous ballet choreographer, and a Greater Manchester town whose full name adds 'under Lyne', heard as 'under strain'

explanation.surface: A celebrated ballet figure whom people in Manchester mention with great emphasis.
explanation.walkthrough: Sadler's Wells is a London theatre linked with the Royal Ballet; Ashton-under-Lyne is a town near Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Frederick Ashton was founder choreographer of the Royal Ballet, which began at Sadler's Wells.
